title: Sample-Optimal Estimation of the Fréchet Inception Distance

paper.title: Sample-Optimal Estimation of the Fréchet Inception Distance
paper.abstract:
Abstract The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) is widely used to evaluate generative models, but its empirical plug-in estimator suffers from finite-sample bias [ 4 , 7 ] . We study the sample complexity n n of estimating FID to error ϵ \epsilon between d d -dimensional Gaussians with bounded mean distance and covariances, when one distribution is known. Our contributions are threefold. 1. We establish tight finite-sample Θ ⁡ ( d 2 n ) \Theta(\frac{d^{2}}{n}) bias and Θ ⁡ ( d n + d 2 n 2 ) \Theta(\frac{d}{n}+\frac{d^{2}}{n^{2}}) variance bounds for the empirical plug-in estimator, establishing a ≳ d 2 \gtrsim d^{2} sample complexity. 2. To debias the empirical plug-in estimator, we generalize the FID ∞ \mathrm{FID}_{\infty} estimator of [ 7 ] to extrapolation methods of arbitrary order k k . We further prove tight bias and variance bounds of Θ ⁡ ( d k + 2 n k + 1 ) \Theta(\frac{d^{k+2}}{n^{k+1}}) and Θ ⁡ ( d n + d 2 n 2 ) \Theta(\frac{d}{n}+\frac{d^{2}}{n^{2}}) for any order- k k extrapolation under our framework. 3. We introduce Relative Taylor Debiasing (RTD), a new, computationally efficient FID estimation algorithm using debiasing techniques inspired by U-statistics. We show that RTD achieves an O ⁡ ( d ϵ 2 ) O(\frac{d}{\epsilon^{2}}) sample complexity, and prove that this is optimal. We provide a complementary empirical evaluation of our new estimators.
Our experiments on synthetic Gaussians validate the predicted residual bias and support the tightness of our bounds. On ImageNet with Inception embeddings, RTD achieves the lowest mean estimation error at the standard 50K sample budget, while our second-order variance-aware extrapolation estimator (VALE 2 ) uses only 10K samples to achieve accuracy comparable to FID ∞ at 50K samples. 1 1 1 Authors are ordered alphabetically. 2 2 2 Our code is available at https://github.com/zys996/sample-optimal-fid-estimation .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A central challenge in generative modeling scholarship is evaluation : that is, how can we quantitatively judge the quality of a model’s generations? Without evaluation, it is difficult to make concrete comparisons between different methods, algorithms, and architectures. Downstream performance can sometimes be used as a proxy for quality, but many settings, notably image generation, where the ultimate goal is to produce high-quality natural images, require metrics that serve as direct proxies for generative quality. While there is no perfect metric for this task, the Fréchet inception distance (FID), introduced in [ 10 ] , has become a standard tool for this purpose. The FID is a measure of distance between distributions P , Q P,Q over image embeddings. Formally, let P P , Q Q be distributions over images passed through a fixed embedding (often the Inception network [ 28 ] ). When P = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝁 , 𝐀 ) P={\mathcal{N}}(\boldsymbol{\mu},{\mathbf{A}}) and Q = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝂 , 𝐁 ) Q={\mathcal{N}}(\boldsymbol{\nu},{\mathbf{B}}) are multivariate Gaussians, their FID is exactly the squared 2 2 -Wasserstein distance W 2 2 ​ ( P , Q ) W_{2}^{2}(P,Q) , and enjoys the parametric form d FID ​ ( P , Q ) := ‖ 𝝁 − 𝝂 ‖ 2 2 + Tr ​ ( 𝐀 ) + Tr ​ ( 𝐁 ) − 2 ​ Tr ​ ( ( 𝐀 1 / 2 ​ 𝐁𝐀 1 / 2 ) 1 / 2 ) , \textup{d}_{\mathrm{FID}}(P,Q):=\left\lVert\boldsymbol{\mu}-\boldsymbol{\nu}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+\textup{Tr}({\mathbf{A}})+\textup{Tr}({\mathbf{B}})-2\textup{Tr}\left(\left({\mathbf{A}}^{1/2}{\mathbf{B}}{\mathbf{A}}^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}\right), (1) see [ 9 ] . For non-Gaussian P , Q P,Q , it is typical to take d FID ​ ( P , Q ) \textup{d}_{\mathrm{FID}}(P,Q) to be the FID between the multivariate Gaussians with matched means and covariances to P P and Q Q . In practice, the FID is estimated from a finite dataset of samples. The empirical plug-in estimator , which simply evaluates ( 1 ) on empirical means and covariances, is perhaps the most commonly used estimator. Unfortunately, this estimator exhibits a substantial finite-sample bias, particularly in high-dimensional spaces. For example, [ 4 ] construct a 2048 2048 -dimensional, exactly Gaussian example in which FID estimates constructed using 50,000 samples consistently give the wrong ordering between distributions. Recent studies of modern generative models likewise report that FID-based conclusions depend substantially on the sample size [ 7 , 12 ] . Thus, finite-sample bias is a well-documented issue when benchmarking with the FID. It can materially affect comparisons between generative models, even at practical scales, and removing it often requires the user to generate many images, which becomes extremely costly, especially if evaluation is repeated throughout model development. This motivates our central question. Can we characterize the sample complexity of estimating the FID? A precursor to our work, [ 7 ] , also investigated this question, and proposed an alternative estimator called FID ∞ \mathrm{FID}_{\infty} . They further empirically demonstrated that FID ∞ \mathrm{FID}_{\infty} attains an improved sample complexity compared to the empirical plug-in estimator, at a fixed error level. However, [ 7 ] does not prove non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for either the plug-in estimator or FID ∞ \mathrm{FID}_{\infty} , leaving open the possibility of improved estimators in both theory and practice.

sections.text: W 2 W_{2} estimation with provable guarantees. The statistical properties of empirical plug-in estimators for Gaussian W 2 W_{2} and W 2 2 W_{2}^{2} distances have been studied in several prior works. For example, [ 24 ] establish asymptotic limit laws for W 2 2 W_{2}^{2} , without finite-sample guarantees, and [ 36 ] obtain an O ⁡ ( d 2 ϵ 2 ) O(\frac{d^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}) sample complexity for W 2 W_{2} estimation, assuming that the covariance spectra are bounded away from zero. This requirement is avoided by [ 11 ] , who give a sample complexity of O ⁡ ( d 5 ϵ 4 ) O(\frac{d^{5}}{\epsilon^{4}}) for W 2 2 W_{2}^{2} estimation. Beyond the empirical plug-in estimator, alternative estimators aim to improve sample efficiency: [ 31 , 32 ] develop random matrix corrections for W 2 2 W_{2}^{2} estimation, but establish only asymptotic guarantees. For general smooth nonlinear functionals, extrapolation and Taylor debiasing methods have been analyzed by [ 15 , 14 ] . However, smoothness assumptions do not hold uniformly for W 2 2 W_{2}^{2} estimation when singular covariances are allowed, and the resulting sample complexities incur a polynomial factor in the inverse-smallest eigenvalue, which we avoid. FID evaluation and debiasing. Since its introduction by [ 10 ] , FID has become a standard metric for evaluating generative models [ 23 , 30 , 12 ] . Despite its popularity, subsequent works identify limitations and propose improvements along two directions. One concerns finite-sample error , e.g., [ 7 ] propose FID ∞ \mathrm{FID}_{\infty} , which extrapolates FID scores in inverse sample size using a Taylor expansion heuristic. Their experiments support the underlying assumption and demonstrate empirical improvements, but they do not establish a rigorous finite-sample guarantee of FID ∞ \mathrm{FID}_{\infty} ’s improvement over the empirical plug-in estimator. Another direction questions the representational power of Inception embeddings. Prior work explores alternative representations such as CLIP [ 16 ] and DINOv2 [ 26 ] to address limitations of Inception features in perceptual evaluation. [ 12 ] empirically show that image distributions in Inception feature space are multimodal and violate the Gaussian assumption. They also expose FID’s vulnerability to manipulation: deliberately constructed image distortions can improve FID scores while degrading image quality. To mitigate this issue, MMD-based alternatives that avoid the Gaussian assumption have been proposed, including KID [ 4 ] and CMMD [ 12 ] .

4 Estimation via Extrapolation
sections.text: Theorem 1 shows that the suboptimal sample complexity of the plug-in estimator arises from its large bias at sample sizes n ≪ d 2 n\ll d^{2} . In this section, we study extrapolation as a principled strategy for debiasing FID estimation, by generalizing the FID ∞ \mathrm{FID}_{\infty} estimator of [ 7 ] to higher orders. In Section 4.1 , we first give a generic framework for bounding the bias of estimators constructed via extrapolation. In Section 4.2 , we specialize this framework to FID estimation, and in Section 4.3 , we discuss strategies for choosing extrapolation weights in practice. Finally, we demonstrate sharpness of our bias bound from Section 4.2 at every fixed order in Section 4.4 .

sections.heading: 7 ImageNet Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate the practical accuracy and sample efficiency of RTD and extrapolation methods on ImageNet. Extrapolations involve several tunable hyperparameters, so we begin with hyperparameter selection on the development pool. We then compare RTD and optimized VALE against the empirical estimator and FID ∞ under standard 50K-sample setup. Finally, we reduce the sample budget to assess which estimators maintain robust performance with fewer samples. Experimental setup. We evaluate FID estimation on ImageNet using seven generator checkpoints spanning GAN, diffusion, and autoregressive models [ 25 , 13 , 35 , 30 ] , with Inception-V3, DINOv2, and CLIP embeddings [ 10 , 26 , 12 ] . For each checkpoint, 550K pictures are generated in total: the first 300K form a development pool for proxy construction and ablation, and the remaining 250K is evenly split into five held-out blocks. Details are provided in Appendix D.2 . Reference proxies. Since population distances are unknown, we evaluate sensitivity to three reference proxies computed on the full 300K development pool: the empirical plug-in estimate Q c plug Q_{c}^{\mathrm{plug}} , FID ∞ Q c ∞ Q_{c}^{\infty} , and RTD Q c Q_{c} , for each checkpoint–embedding pair c c . The latter two are medians of five randomized estimates on the same pool. Figure 3 compares StyleGAN-XL-256 across Inception-V3, DINOv2, and CLIP over 30K–300K samples. The empirical estimates remain noticeably higher, whereas RTD and FID ∞ broadly agree across the tested sample budgets. Additional results for the remaining checkpoints and all three embeddings appear in Appendix D.3 .
